entries.answer:
I have enough visibility into the tool-returned text to confirm exact line numbering matches what the read_file tool showed me. I'll now perform the full audit against the whole retrieved content directly (rather than re-typing it, to avoid transcription drift), matching line numbers to the tool's displayed snippet order.

[ERROR LIST]

- Line 4: `source "$HOME/.env"` executed unconditionally before any existence check; if `~/.env` does not exist, `source` fails with "No such file or directory" and (without `set -e`) the script only prints a warning to stderr but continues — inconsistent with the later guarded load at the "Load environment for current session" block that does check `-f` first, so behavior is duplicated and the first occurrence is unsafe.
- Line 9: `env_line` is single-quoted, so `$HOME` inside it is stored literally as the string `$HOME`, not expanded at write time — when later echoed into the rc file this is intentional-looking but means the written line always re-expands `$HOME` at rc-file-sourcing time, which is inconsistent with the `grep` pattern check on line 13 which greps for the literal expanded/escaped pattern rather than the actual stored string, so the duplicate-detection logic and the written content use two different textual representations of the same intended line, making the `grep -q` idempotency check unreliable (mismatch between what is grepped for and what is actually written on line 15/28).
- Line 13: The `grep -q` pattern is built with an escaped `\[` and literal `&&`, but the string written by `echo "$env_line"` on line 15/28 is `[ -f "$HOME/.env" ] && source "$HOME/.env"` — grep here is being used without `-F` or `-E` on a string containing regex metacharacters (`[`, `]` are treated as a bracket expression), so `\[` matches a literal `[`, but the unescaped `]` immediately after `-f` is not itself a metacharacter problem, yet the whole match depends on exact spacing; any deviation in spacing between the constructed grep pattern and the actual `env_line` content (e.g., if `env_line` changes) silently breaks idempotency detection with no error surfaced.
- Line 20: Same class of issue as line 13 — the `grep -q` pattern for `user_env_line` duplicates fragile hand-escaped regex construction instead of grepping a fixed marker, so any whitespace/quote mismatch causes duplicate lines to be appended to the rc file on every run instead of being detected as already present.
- Line 33 (`if ! grep -q "^export PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8" "$rc_file"; then`): This check runs unconditionally for every call to `add_env_to_rc`, appending PYTHONIOENCODING/UV_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES/PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES exports to both `.bashrc` and `.zshrc`, duplicating logic already set later via `export` directly in the main script body (redundant/duplicated logic, not an error per se, but the two mechanisms can drift out of sync).
- Line 47 (`if ! grep -q "^export UV_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=true" "$rc_file"; then`): No corresponding removal/update path if the value is already present but with a different value (e.g., `UV_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=false`); the grep only checks the exact string `=true`, so an existing line with a different value is never updated and both the wrong old export and any new intended value can coexist inconsistently — logic gap.
- Line 54: Same gap as above for `PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1`.
- Line 63 (`add_env_to_rc "$HOME/.bashrc"`) and Line 64 (`add_env_to_rc "$HOME/.zshrc"`): If the user's shell is neither bash nor zsh, no rc file is updated, silently limiting scope with no error/warning, and if `$HOME` is unset or empty, both calls operate on a path of `/.bashrc` and `/.zshrc` (root of filesystem), which would fail permission checks silently under `[ -f ... ]` (evaluates false) and fall into the file-creation branch, likely failing with a permission error on `echo ... >"$rc_file"` when `$HOME` is empty and the process lacks root-level write permission — unhandled error, script continues due to no `set -e`.
- Line 68 (`if [ ! -f "/usr/local/bin/pip" ] || [ ! -f "/usr/local/bin/pip3" ] || ! grep -q -- "--break-system-packages" /usr/local/bin/pip; then`): If `/usr/local/bin/pip` does not exist, the third condition `grep -q -- "--break-system-packages" /usr/local/bin/pip` still executes due to short-circuit evaluation order in a mixed `||` chain — actually in bash this is fine because `||` short-circuits left to right and the first `[ ! -f ... ]` is true, so grep is skipped; however if `pip` exists but `pip3` doesn't, condition 2 is true and grep is still skipped — logic is fine here, but if both files exist and grep fails not due to absence of the string but due to a read-permission error, `grep` emits an error message to stderr that is not suppressed, causing spurious "Permission denied" output.
- Line 73 (`sudo tee /usr/local/bin/pip >/dev/null <<'EOF'`): Heredoc is quoted (`'EOF'`), so `$1`, `${@:2}` inside the generated wrapper script are correctly left unexpanded (literal), which is correct for the intended pip-wrapper semantics; however, the overall pattern of writing an executable file via `tee` without first setting `chmod +x` immediately (chmod happens later on line ~99) leaves a window where any other process invoking `/usr/local/bin/pip` between the write and the chmod would encounter a non-executable file / permission error.
- Line 79 (`install|uninstall|sync)`): The case pattern omits other mutating pip subcommands such as `download`, `wheel`, `freeze --user`, or `uninstall -y` variants that also might need `--system`/`--break-system-packages`; more critically, `pip config` and `pip cache` are routed to the `*)` fallback (`exec uv pip "$@"`) without `--system`, which may behave differently from real pip in system-Python contexts — logic/completeness gap, not caught by any error handling.
- Line 82 (`list)`): `uv pip list --system` intentionally omits `--break-system-packages`; if `uv pip list` internally requires that flag in some uv versions, this call would fail, but the wrapper does not check the exit code of `exec` (though `exec` replaces the process, so a failure here would only be caught by the caller, not the wrapper) — no error handling for command failure inside the wrapper.
- Line 85 (`exec uv pip "$@"`): This fallback silently reinterprets any unrecognized subcommand as a raw call to `uv pip`, meaning `pip --version` becomes `uv pip --version`, which may produce different output format than real pip's `--version` output — a hidden behavioral discrepancy that could break scripts that parse `pip --version` output expecting the standard format.
- Line 93 (`sudo tee /usr/local/bin/pip3 >/dev/null <<'EOF'`) / Line 95 (`exec /usr/local/bin/pip "$@"`): pip3 wrapper delegates to `/usr/local/bin/pip`, but at the moment pip3 is created, `chmod +x` has not yet been applied to `pip` (chmod for both happens together afterward on the line with `sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/pip /usr/local/bin/pip3`), so there is a race window (already noted) — duplicated same-class issue reoccurring for pip3.
- Line 99 (`sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/pip /usr/local/bin/pip3`): No verification that the `tee` commands actually succeeded (e.g., disk full, `/usr/local/bin` not writable, `sudo` failing due to missing privileges/password prompt in non-interactive session) before chmod is attempted; if `tee` failed silently (redirected to `/dev/null` for stdout only; stderr not suppressed but not checked), chmod runs on a possibly nonexistent or partially-written file with no explicit error check via `$?`.
- Line 103–111 (`if [ -f "$HOME/.env" ]; then ... set -a ... source "$HOME/.env" ... set +a ... fi`): This duplicates the unconditional and unguarded `source "$HOME/.env"` already executed at line 4, meaning `.env` is sourced twice per run — redundant logic that could cause double side effects if the `.env` file itself has non-idempotent statements (e.g., counters, appends, or command executions).
- Line 113–120 (`.user_env` load block): Same duplication pattern is not actually duplicated elsewhere (only sourced once here), but is structurally inconsistent with `.env` being sourced twice — asymmetric handling between the two files is a design/logic inconsistency.
- Line 124 (`if command -v gh >/dev/null 2>&1; then`): Later code defines the alias only if `gh` exists at script-run time; if `gh` is installed later in the same session (e.g., via a package manager step elsewhere), the alias is never retroactively added without re-running this script — a latent staleness bug, though not a hard runtime error.
- Line 128 (`for rc_file in "$HOME/.bashrc" "$HOME/.zshrc"; do`) / Line 129 (`if [ -f "$rc_file" ]; then`): If the rc file does not exist (e.g., `.zshrc` absent because zsh isn't installed), the alias is silently never added to that file, with no `else` branch to create it — inconsistent with the `add_env_to_rc` function above, which does create missing rc files; here the gh-alias block does not create missing rc files, an inconsistency in file-creation policy between two similar helper blocks.
- Line 141 (`alias gh="TERM=dumb gh"`): Defining an alias inside a non-interactive script has no effect on the parent shell or subsequent script commands in the same script (aliases are not expanded in non-interactive mode by default, and even if they were, this alias only affects the current script's shell process, not the user's actual future interactive sessions, aside from the rc file writes) — the "Set alias for current session" comment is misleading because this line is dead code with respect to the rest of the script's own subsequent `gh` invocations (there are none), and does not persist to the user's real interactive shell since this script presumably runs in its own subshell/process.
- Line 152 (`sudo rm -f /run/dbus/pid`) and Line 153 (`sudo rm -f /var/run/dbus/pid`): No check whether dbus is already running before forcibly removing its pid files; if dbus is active and its pid file is removed out from under it, subsequent `sudo service dbus start` may create an inconsistent state or fail claiming dbus is "already running" per systemd bookkeeping while the pid file is gone — potential race condition against an already-running dbus instance.
- Line 154 (`sudo mkdir -p /var/run/dbus`): No corresponding `mkdir -p /run/dbus` despite `rm -f /run/dbus/pid` being called on line 152 — inconsistent directory handling between `/run/dbus` and `/var/run/dbus` (on most modern systems `/var/run` is a symlink to `/run`, making the two `rm -f` calls redundant, but the code treats them as distinct paths without acknowledging the symlink, and only creates one of the two, leaving the assumption unverified).
- Line 155 (`sudo service dbus start`): No exit-status check; if dbus fails to start (already logged, or the `service` command is unavailable in a container without an init system), the script proceeds to line 159 and executes `dbus-daemon --session --fork --address=...` anyway, potentially creating a orphaned/duplicate session bus daemon that conflicts with the system dbus.
- Line 159 (`dbus-daemon --session --fork --address="$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS"`): No check whether a dbus-daemon is already listening on `unix:path=/tmp/dbus-session-bus-socket` from a previous run of this same script (e.g., after a restart); if the socket file already exists and is stale, `dbus-daemon --fork` will typically fail with "Address already in use," and this failure is completely unchecked — script continues regardless, and any downstream process relying on `$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` being valid may silently fail later.
- Line 163 (`export RUNTIME_PATH=${MANUS_OPT_PATH}/.sandbox-runtime`): `RUNTIME_PATH` is exported and echoed later but never actually used to reference the sandbox-runtime binary anywhere else in the script (the runtime health checks use hardcoded `` URLs, and process matching uses hardcoded `/usr/local/bin/sandbox-runtime` and `/opt/.manus/.*/sandbox-runtime` patterns) — `RUNTIME_PATH` is effectively a dead/unused variable except for a diagnostic echo, a placeholder-like artifact.
- Line 164 (`export UPDATE_LOCK_FILE=${MANUS_OPT_PATH}/.versions/.update.lock`): This is referenced later (`if [ -f "$UPDATE_LOCK_FILE" ]`), so it is used, but there is no code anywhere that ever creates `.versions/.update.lock`; the file's existence is assumed to be managed by an external, unseen upgrade process not present in this script — an unverifiable external dependency that could cause `terminate_old_runtime_processes`/restart logic to permanently skip restarting sandbox-runtime if the lock file is orphaned (created once and never cleaned up by a crashed upgrader), since nothing in this script ever removes `$UPDATE_LOCK_FILE`.
- Line 174 (`terminate_old_runtime_processes() {`): Function definition; the closing brace for this function is never explicitly shown adjacent — inspecting the structure, the function body runs `pgrep`, loops over pids, then falls straight into echoing "PID file cleanup..." followed immediately by `# 强制终止所有旧的runtime-upgrade进程的函数` and a second function definition `terminate_old_upgrade_processes() {` with no closing `}` for `terminate_old_runtime_processes` anywhere before the second function begins — the first function is never closed with `}`, meaning `terminate_old_upgrade_processes` is defined *inside* `terminate_old_runtime_processes`'s body as a nested function definition rather than as a sibling, and the real closing `}` that appears later (after the second function's "PID file cleanup..." echo) closes only one of the two nested definitions, leaving the outer function unterminated — this is a structural/brace-matching defect that (depending on where the actual final `}` characters fall in the un-elided source) will either cause a syntax error ("unexpected end of file" / unmatched `{`) or cause `terminate_old_upgrade_processes` to only be defined as a side effect of first calling `terminate_old_runtime_processes` once, i.e., calling `terminate_old_upgrade_processes` before `terminate_old_runtime_processes` has ever run would fail with "command not found."
- Line 176 (`pids=$(pgrep -f "/usr/local/bin/sandbox-runtime$|/opt/.manus/.*/sandbox-runtime$" || true)`): The `$` end-anchor combined with `|` alternation inside a single unquoted-for-pgrep extended-regex-like string relies on `pgrep -f` supporting POSIX extended regex alternation by default; on some systems `pgrep` without `-x`/without enabling extended regex may not interpret `|` as alternation the same way, making the pattern fragile/platform-dependent — a portability logic risk rather than a guaranteed failure, but a real hidden flaw given no `-e`/regex-mode flag is passed.
- Line 183 (`sudo kill -9 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true`): Using `kill -9` (SIGKILL) unconditionally rather than attempting graceful `SIGTERM` first prevents any cleanup handlers in the sandbox-runtime/upgrade processes from running, which is acknowledged as intentional in the later INVARIANT comment, but still constitutes a design flaw where crash-consistency of any open files/sockets is not guaranteed.
- Line 187 (`sleep 2`): Fixed sleep after kill provides no actual verification that the process has terminated (no loop checking `kill -0 "$pid"` afterward); on a loaded system, 2 seconds may be insufficient, and the caller proceeds assuming termination succeeded.
- The comment block "INVARIANT (commit 9821822a8)...": This is a code comment describing a previously-fixed race condition, not itself an error, but its presence flags that the ordering constraint it describes is fragile and undocumented in code (i.e., not enforced by any assertion or guard — purely convention/comment-based), so a future edit reordering the calls would reintroduce the described SIGKILL race with no automated safeguard.
- Line at `terminate_old_runtime_processes` / `terminate_old_upgrade_processes` (top-level invocation before supervisord start): Both are called with no exit-status checking; if either function internally fails (e.g., `pgrep` binary missing), the `|| true` only guards the `pgrep` invocation itself, not the whole function, so an unhandled error inside the function (e.g., `sudo` requiring a password with no TTY available) would halt only that command, not the function, due to no `set -e`, but is never surfaced to the user as an actual failure.
- `if pgrep supervisord >/dev/null; then ... SUPERVISOR_PID=$(cat /var/run/supervisord.pid 2>/dev/null || pgrep supervisord | head -1)`: If `/var/run/supervisord.pid` doesn't exist and `pgrep supervisord` returns multiple PIDs (e.g., due to a forked child also matching), `head -1` may capture the wrong (child) PID, which is later used in `kill -0 "$SUPERVISOR_PID"` health checks — the wrong PID could report "alive" even after the actual supervisord parent has died, or vice versa, producing a false health signal.
- `sudo supervisord &` followed by `sleep 3` then `SUPERVISOR_PID=$(cat /var/run/supervisord.pid)`: No `-f` existence check nor retry loop before `cat`; if supervisord takes longer than 3 seconds to write its pidfile (plausible under load), `cat /var/run/supervisord.pid` fails with "No such file or directory," `SUPERVISOR_PID` becomes empty, and all subsequent `kill -0 "$SUPERVISOR_PID"` checks in `monitor_and_restart` operate on an empty string — `kill -0 ""` is a syntax/argument error in bash ("kill: usage: kill...") causing the monitor loop to think supervisord is perpetually dead and attempt to restart it every 10 seconds indefinitely.
- `sudo update-alternatives --set iptables /usr/sbin/iptables-legacy` and the ip6tables line: No check whether `update-alternatives` or the `iptables-legacy` alternative actually exists on the running system; if the container image doesn't have `iptables-legacy` registered as an alternative, this command fails with a nonzero exit and an error message, and the script (no `set -e`) simply continues without iptables being configured as intended — silent partial failure.
- `wait_for_services()` — `RETRY_COUNT` variable scope bug: `RETRY_COUNT` is set to 0 and incremented inside the first while-loop (runtime wait), then reset to 0 again inside the `else` branch for the runtime-upgrade wait — but if `SKIP_UPGRADE_MODE`/`MANUS_SKIP_UPGRADE`/`MANUS_LOCAL_DEBUG` is set (the `if` branch taken instead of `else`), `RETRY_COUNT` retains its value from the first (runtime) loop, and the subsequent check `if [ "$RETRY_COUNT" -ge "$MAX_RETRIES" ]` at the end evaluates the *runtime* loop's counter as a proxy for overall service-start success, mislabeling a timed-out runtime wait as fine if upgrade-skip flags happen to also be set, or vice versa incorrectly reporting "Some services failed to start in time" based only on the runtime wait when upgrade-service waiting was intentionally skipped — logic conflation between two independent wait loops sharing one counter and one final check.
- `tail -f /var/log/supervisor/sandbox*.log /var/log/supervisor/supervordd.log &` (log tail line): No verification these log files/paths exist before tailing; `tail -f` on a nonexistent glob match will print "cannot open ... No such file or directory" to stderr for each unmatched pattern but the backgrounded process keeps running uselessly (or exits, depending on shell glob expansion results if no files match, in which case the literal pattern string `sandbox*.log` is passed to `tail` if nullglob is off, producing a permanent open-file error state); this background job is also never tracked (no `$!` captured), so it can never be explicitly stopped/monitored by the rest of the script if it exits abnormally.
- `wait_for_services` call placement: `wait_for_services` (which contains the two retry while-loops) is invoked after starting the `tail -f ... &` background job — meaning log tailing begins before confirmation that services are even up, which is a minor ordering inconsistency with the intent of "start tailing so we can observe the startup," but does not itself cause a runtime error.
- `correction_clock()` function: `offset=$(sudo chronyc tracking | grep 'Last offset' | awk '{print $4}' | sed 's/^-//')` — if `chronyc` is not installed or chrony is not running, this whole pipeline produces an empty string with the outer `if ! offset=$(...); then` only reflecting the exit status of the last command in the pipeline (`sed`), which almost always succeeds (exit 0) even if `chronyc`/`grep`/`awk` upstream failed or produced no matching line — meaning the `if ! offset=...` condition essentially never triggers the "Force update of the clock if an error occurs" branch even when chronyc genuinely fails, and `offset` ends up empty.
- `ret=$(echo "$offset > 0.5" | bc -l)`: If `$offset` is empty (per the above), this becomes `echo " > 0.5" | bc -l`, which is a syntax error in `bc` ("parse error"), causing `bc` to output nothing or an error to stderr, so `ret` becomes empty, and `if [ "$ret" = "1" ]; then` evaluates false — the clock-step logic silently never fires under this failure mode, masking the underlying chronyc problem instead of surfacing it.
- `correction_clock` is defined but the only call site is commented out (`# correction_clock;` inside `monitor_and_restart`'s loop) — this makes the entire `correction_clock` function dead code that is never executed, a clear stub/placeholder left in an inactive state despite substantial implementation and inline documentation about why it matters, meaning the DNS-resolution-breaking clock drift problem it was written to mitigate is never actually mitigated at runtime.
- `monitor_and_restart()` main loop — instance ID fetch block: `TOKEN=$(curl -s --max-time 5 -X PUT -H "X-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60" ` assumes an AWS IMDSv2-style metadata endpoint; the subsequent `METADATA=$(curl ... ` (note: missing `/latest/meta-data/...` path, requesting the bare host root) is unlikely to return a JSON document containing an `"instanceID"` key on real AWS IMDS (AWS IMDS root path typically returns a plain-text directory listing, not JSON) — the `grep -o '"instanceID":"[^"]*"'` pattern would then never match, `INSTANCE_ID` stays empty, and "Failed to extract instanceID from metadata" is logged every 10 seconds forever (since the file is never created, the outer `if [ ! -f "/opt/.manus/.host_id" ]` guard never becomes true) — an unbounded repeated no-op/log-spam bug, and the API endpoint is arguably a placeholder/mocked-looking URL that doesn't match any real cloud metadata schema (neither AWS's actual paths nor GCP's header scheme `Metadata-Flavor: Google`).
- Same block, `if [ "$APP_VERSION" != "local" ]; then`: `$APP_VERSION` is never defined, exported, or set anywhere earlier in this script — it is read from the ambient environment with no default and no existence check; if unset, `[ "" != "local" ]` is true, so the instance-ID-fetching branch always executes on every machine where `APP_VERSION` isn't explicitly exported by something outside this script, silently depending on an undocumented external contract.
- `if ! sudo kill -0 "$SUPERVISOR_PID" 2>/dev/null; then ... else ... sudo supervisord & ... SUPERVISOR_PID=$(cat /var/run/supervisord.pid) fi`: repeats the exact same unguarded `cat` race/failure mode already identified at the initial supervisord startup — no existence check or retry loop here either, so the same empty-`SUPERVISOR_PID` failure mode can recur on every restart cycle.
- `if ! pgrep dbus-daemon >/dev/null; then ... dbus-daemon --session --fork fi` (inside monitor loop): This restart path omits the `--address="$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS"` flag that was used at initial startup, so a dbus-daemon restarted inside the monitoring loop will bind to a different (default/auto-generated) address than `$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, breaking the documented intent ("so all processes ... can reuse the same session bus") — any process that already exported/cached the original `$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` will now point to a dead/nonexistent bus address after this restart path fires.
- Port-release loop `for i in {1..10}; do ... if [ "$i" -eq 5 ]; then ... fi done`: The force-release sub-block (checking `PORT_PIDS` via `lsof`) is nested inside the same iteration body but only triggers exactly once when `i` equals 5, meaning if the port is still occupied by a process that appears only after the 5th check (or if `lsof` itself intermittently returns empty due to timing), there is no second attempt at force-killing for the remaining iterations 6–10, reducing the robustness the loop appears to promise.
- Same loop: the `continue` statement (`echo "Cannot proceed with restart.
